speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROGRESS OP ALLIED OPERATIONS-PARTICIPATION OP CANADIAN FORCES
speechtext:
Since the statement I made a week ago on the military operations in Sicily, the offensive of the united nations has been intensified on a number of fronts. Our main interest at the moment naturally centres in Sicily, where Canadian forces are engaged. Before touching upon the progress that has since been made in Sicily, a word about the other theatres, in which there had been significant developments, may not be out of place.
In Russia, after sharp fighting and heavy German losses, the nazi summer offensive was quickly halted. In its stead, the Soviet army and air force have developed1 a powerful offensive against Orel. This strategic centre has been under German control for nearly two years. It is one of the most strongly fortified positions of the central front. The battle for Orel is a dramatic reminder of Russia's share in the total military effort of the united nations.
At the other side of the world, in the southwest Pacific, the present month has seen a sustained attack by Australian and United States forces against Japanese strongholds in New Guinea. In the Solomon islands, the United States forces have advanced northward, and are in fact besieging the main Japanese air base in that area. As more stepping stones are wrested from the Japanese, the offensive will be intensified against all the outlying areas north of Australia now under Japanese control.
In the northern Pacific, the Aleutian area has also seen heavier bombings of Japanese targets by United States and Canadian squadrons.	Kiska,	the last remaining
Japanese outpost, an immediate menace to both Canada and the United States, is being attacked whenever weather conditions are favourable. Until the Japanese are driven out of Kiska, we may expect continued fighting in this area.
In the battle of the Atlantic, the arrangement for increased escorts by sea, and continuous cover by air, which have been in effect for some three months, have more than justified expectations.

Coming to the Mediterranean area, two weeks have now passed since the allied forces landed in Sicily. The second week of the invasion witnessed a continuation of the steady advance of the previous week. Town after town surrendered1. Within the week, the number of axis prisoners taken increased to well over 50,000. The allied invasion forces extended their occupation from one-third to more than two-thirds of the island. Throughout, Canada's troops took a foremost part in the fighting. Their skill and determination have called forth the commendation of both General Montgomery and General Alexander.
At the beginning of the week, after joining forces at Enna, which is the hub of communications in central Sicily, Canadian and American formations continued to press north. Yesterday an American armoured division captured Palermo, the historic capital and largest city in Sicily. By the capture of Palermo, and the advances of American and Canadian units, large numbers of axis forces have been trapped in the western half of the island. Northeast of Enna, Canadian units encountered strong German resistance. Other of our forces have been taking part in the eighth army's tightening encirclement of Catania. The fall of Catania, which may be expected at any time, will compel the retreat of the axis forces towards Messina and the mainland of Italy. That retreat will lead inevitably to the occupation of the whole of Sicily.
The allied land advances on the island were supported throughout the week by intense allied air activity over the island and the Italian mainland. In these aerial operations, the Royal Canadian Air Force continued to play an important part. A Royal Canadian Air Force fighter squadron-a self-contained Canadian unit of the middle east forces-is now based on Sicily, and for some days has been operating in support of the forward elements of the allied armies. The hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. Sinclair) is adjutant of this squadron. There are, as well, in Sicily, many R.CAJF. personnel not included in this squadron, but attached to RA.F. units. During the week our bomber units, operating with General Doolittle's force in North Africa, participated in raids on Sicily and on the Italian mainland.
A week ago I referred to the officers and men of the Royal Canadian navy who took part in the landing operations in Sicily. Quite a number of these men are veterans of Dieppe and North Africa. They are still continuing to assist in landing supplies and reinforcements at different ports.

Old Age Pensions
General McNaughton, who has just returned to England from the Mediterranean area, has described the assault upon Sicily as the most perfect example of combined operations in history. This statement is, in part, a merited tribute to the rigorous training and patient waiting of the Canadian forces which have served the longest under General McNaugh-ton's command.
A significant development of the past week in Sicily was the establishment of an allied military government of the occupied territory. General Sir Harold Alexander was appointed military governor. In his first proclamation, General Alexander declared that the purpose of the allies was to deliver the people from the fascist regime, and restore Italy as a land of free people. He ordered the dissolution of all fascist organizations. In this proclamation will be found the basis upon which the allied nations aim to effect the liberation of Europe from Axis aggression, and from fascist domination.
A year ago, when parliament adjourned, the united nations had experienced nearly eight months of reverses and setbacks. This continent was immediately threatened from the west. On the east, enemy U-boats ranged destructively along our coast, and into the gulf and river St. Lawrence. As we leave today for our homes, we will carry with us very different impressions. The tide has definitely turned. Everywhere the forces of freedom have the initiative.
While our fears about its outcome have lessened, the war, in a more immediate way, has been brought closer than ever to us. All arms of our fighting services are now in the thick of the conflict. Our fighting men are certain to continue in action on many fronts, until the enemy has surrendered. No one can say for how long that may be. Our men face a terrible ordeal of battle. Until victory is achieved, above all else, they must command a singleness of purpose in our hearts and minds, and the utmost that our country can give in their support.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OP INCREASE OF MAXIMUM PAYMENT FROM $20 TO $25 A MONTH
speechtext:
I wish to make a brief announcement on pensions for the aged and blind.
Early in the war we had a number of representations made, not only in this house but elsewhere, that the $20 maximum monthly pension payable under the Old Age Pension Act was too low under present conditions and
should be increased either by adding to it the cost of living bonus or by some flat increase, say, to $25 per month.	On
November 14, 1941, I made a statement in this house announcing the government's policy in respect to these representations. In particular, I pointed out that there were substantial variations in cost of living and economic conditions as between the various provinces and in public opinion or social outlook amongst the people of the various provinces as to what is a reasonable amount of non-contributory pension to be paid to aged and blind persons; that several provinces were still paying considerably less than the maximum pension allowable under the act, and there was therefore in such provinces considerable leeway for increasing the average pension paid if the province felt it justifiable; and that in view of the colossal burden of war expenditure which the dominion was having to carry whereas the position of the provincial governments had greatly improved as a result of these war expenditures, it seemed only fair and reasonable that those provinces which felt that a higher pension should be paid should themselves pay it out of their own resources. I, therefore, indicated that if any of the provinces desired to supplement the old age pension paid in that province under our act, we would undertake to amend the regulations in such a way as to assure that such supplementary payments made by a province would not entail a reduction in the pension payable under our act.
Following this suggestion, I went on to say:
Indeed the government is prepared to consider going further than this. It believes, for the reasons already outlined, it would be impossible to justify an increase in the maximum rate of pension payable if the whole cost were to be assumed by the dominion, and that such cases as appear to present immediate diificulties can be met by the provinces on the basis of established individual need. If, nevertheless, all or substantially all the provinces should make representations to the dominion government in favour of some increase in the maximum amount of pension payable, the additional cost to be shared between the dominion and the provinces on the same basis as the present cost, I can assure the committee that the government will be prepared to give consideration to such representations.
This was the substance of the policy I announced on November 14, 1941. Since that announcement was made, six provinces have provided for the payment of supplementary pensions: British Columbia and Alberta pay supplementary pensions of $5 a month; Saskatchewan (beginning July 1) and Manitoba of $1.25 a month; Ontario (beginning July 1) a percentage of the amount of pension
Old Age Pensions

paid; and Nova Scotia (beginning June 1) an amount up to $10 a month, based on the merits of the individual case, with limitation of total income, including allowance, to $365 per year.
These provisional supplementary pensions have gone a long way to help the situation in the provinces in which they are being paid. However, in pursuance of the paragraph of my statement which I have just quoted in full, we have received representations from an increasing number of provinces that the maximum pension payable should be raised, the maximum suggested in most cases being $25. On July 12, I received a letter from a province which brought the total number of provinces making such representations up to eight. Since that time the ninth province has made similar representations.
In view of the unanimity of attitude on the part of the provincial governments which has now been established, the dominion has decided that it should make legal provision for increasing the maximum pension payable under the scheme provided for in the act from $20 to $25 per month. There is not time to submit an amendment to the act in the closing hours of the session. Even if there were, as the whole subject of old age pensions and related matters is being studied by the special committee of the House of Commons on social security, it would probably be desirable to wait until a later stage before a legislative amendment making any permanent changes in the act were proposed. We therefore propose to make the provision which I have mentioned by means of an order in council under the War Measures Act.
This order in council will authorize the dominion to enter into supplementary agreements with the provinces, enabling a special war supplement not exceeding $5 per month to be paid, in addition to the regular pension payable under the act as it stands at present. All the terms and conditions under which the present pensions are payable, including the present sharing of the amount of pensions paid in the ratio of 75 per cent and 25 per cent by the dominion and the provinces respectively, and the provisions regarding maximum total income, will be continued, except for the appropriate adjustment in regard to the provisions of the act covering maximum pension and allowable outside income. In so far as the dominion is concerned, the supplementary war pension need not disturb the supplementary pensions now being paid in several of the provinces; that is entirely a matter for the decision of the provincial governments concerned.
IMr. Ilsley.]
It is intended that the new provision will come into operation at the earliest practicable date. It will, however, take a few weeks to work out the necessary supplementary agreements with the provinces and to enable the provinces to set up the necessary machinery for handling the payments.
At March 31, 1943, there were 183,601 old age pensioners and 6,374 blind pensioners, or a total of 189,975. If a supplementary war pension of $5 were paid to all such pensioners the total annual cost would be $11,398,500. The dominion's share, on this basis, would be 75 per cent of this, or $8,548,875 in a full year. Actually, however, total cost and the share of the dominion will be less than this, because in a considerable number of cases outside income accruing to the pensioner will not permit the raising of the present pension, at least not by the full amount of $5 per month.
The extra cost to the dominion will, of course, be a charge against the war appropriation.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. RALSTON (Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subtopic: INCREASES OF PAY FOR WOMEN'S SERVICES
speechtext:
I told the house the other day that I would endeavour to make a statement with regard to the pay of the various women's services in the armed forces. I wish to state that certain increases have been approved with effect July 1, 1943. The basic pay for women will be 80 per cent of that paid men in the armed forces instead of 665 per cent as in the past. Pay for women in all three services will be uniform in the future, and will be increased at the end of four months' and six months' service subject to good conduct and efficiency. That is, pay of the women of the services will start at $1.05 per day and be increased to $1.20 per day at the end of six months' efficient service.
Canadian Forces

In addition to the increase in rates of pay there will be certain other financial benefits available in future. Women will receive trades pay according to their grouping on the same basis and at the same rates as men. Staff and special duty pay will be on the same basis as in the men's branches of the services. Dependents of women in the services other than husbands and children will be eligible for the same rates of dependents' allowances as the dependents of men. That is, dependent parents or other close relatives may receive the allowance.
In future-this is a point which has had a good deal of discussion both outside and in this house-a woman in the services married to another member of the service will not be debarred from receiving dependents' allowance, with the proviso that the woman's total income including the dependents' allowance is not to exceed $2,100, but that those already in the service who have been married for only a short period or who may marry in the future will not receive dependents' allowance until six months after the marriage date.
In the past it has not been permissible for an officer or man in any of the armed services to have the allowance paid to his wife if she too was serving, although it could be made to a wife employed in a civilian capacity.
The maximum income of $2,100 which I have just mentioned in connection with allowances does not include assigned pay.
The increases at the end of four and six months' good service which I have mentioned are similar to those paid soldiers in tlhe army.

speechtext:
On another matter, Mr. Speaker, 1 said I hoped to be able to make some announcement. I am not able to make a statement in detail here, but I can give the outlines of an announcement which will be made in the press as soon as the order is completed. It has to do with arrangements which are being made and authority which is being given with respect to assistance in agricultural operations by certain members of the forces.
Provision is being made to provide assistance in agricultural help, first, by way of compassionate leave, which I think I have already explained to the house and which is applicable in individual cases where there

is hardship in connection with a particular farm or family; second, by detailing men from certain units or certain formations in the armed services to do work as directed by the Department of Labour. It has been decided to decentralize as far as possible this activity. Complaints have been made, and I know that sometimes they are well founded and sometimes the delay could not have been avoided, with regard to the time taken to have certain applications come to headquarters and be dealt with and then further representations asked for. What we are endeavouring to do is to place this matter in the hands of the general officers commanding in the two commands and in the districts. We feel that, with the experience they have had, it ought to be possible for them to bring to bear judgment as to the general uniform policy of the department and at the same time to give consideration to the needs as they exist, along with the necessity of deciding on the ground as to the exigencies of the service and whether men can be spared. So that the new provision which is being made for detailing men is to be administered by the general officers commanding and the district officers commanding. The provision is that men will be detailed -not given leave, and that they cannot be detailed from training centres; that is a sina qua non which we cannot forgo. Prom the operational units men may be detailed up to ten per cent of the strength of the units, and from depots and other formations outside of training centres the percentage is not necessarily limited to ten per cent, but it is as large a percentage as can be spared. In both cases there is a limitation, of course, that it is subject to the exigencies of the service as may be determined by the general officers commanding or the district officers commanding. The detailing is to be done at the request of the director of the dominion-provincial farm labour committee, and I understand he is representing the Department of Labour. The absence which will be provided for will be thirty days. There will be provision for extension if a case is made and if service conditions permit. Pay will be military service pay and allowances, and arrangements, I think, will be made under which, if the going rate in the particular locality is higher than that, it may be possible for the man to get the benefit of that additional rate. That is now being worked out between the Department of Labour and ourselves.
As I say, a fuller statement will be made in the press as soon as all the details are worked out.

speakeroldname: Mr. GORDON GRAYDON (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: There are a couple of questions which I should like to direct to the government if the Prime Minister does not get ahead of me. One is to the Minister of National Defence for Air. Having in mind the minister's previous warning with respect to the anticipated difficulties of obtaining sufficient men for aircrew, coupled with the allegations made in this week's Financial Post that the Canadian air ministry has been battling with army authorities to get priority to enlist category A men for aircrew, will the minister make a statement to the house indicating such changes in the situation as have developed since he last reviewed it for us? I should like also to inquire of the minister as to the steps the government has in mind to avoid this prospective curtailment of the air training programme.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. G. POWER (Minister of National Defence for Air):
speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
My hon. friend was good enough to give me notice of this question, and perhaps I had better proceed by way of a statement.
In January of this year, as a result of an intensive recruiting campaign carried on last autumn, the R.C.A.F. had a substantial reserve of many thousands of volunteers for aircrew training. These were on leave without pay to be called up later on, or employed in duties other than training for aircrew. In order to permit absorption of this reserve and in order that the period before candidates begin training might not be too long, recruiting for aircrew was not urgently pressed during the months of January and February. During the months of April, May and June there has been a noticeable falling-off in the number of those coming forward for aircrew training. In fact, we have now reached the point where we are obtaining less than half our current monthly requirements. We must state frankly that we are seriously alarmed at the lack of recruits coming forward in a constant stream sufficient to meet our current requirements. In other words, at the present time we are "eating our fat" and not building up any reserve strength. That is the situation. Now, as to the steps being taken-

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: That is all right.

speechtext: That, perhaps, would be giving away to the enemy the number of persons whom we propose to train for aircrew during the year, and it would be giving away the battle order.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
As to the steps being taken, we have inaugurated an energetic campaign to recruit aircrew. We are remustering from ground crew within the ranks of the R.C.A.F. a very large number. Last month 761 ground crew were remustered from ground crew to air training. As I have already announced in the house on several occasions, we anticipate that this will be a fruitful source of potential flying men, though I by no means give any guarantee that those remustering will be sufficient to meet our requirements.
It is estimated that there are a very large number of young men of aircrew age and fitness in both essential and unessential industries. Many of these are persons who embarked on an industrial career before they reached the callable age and have since become important cogs in the industrial machine, to such an extent that employers are sometimes reluctant to permit them to enlist, and in some cases have categorized them as key men. An industrial mobilization survey is now being undertaken by the national selective service in all the industrial plants in the dominion. The Royal Canadian Air Force will be repre-
Canadian Air Force

sented on this survey, and has hopes that with the cooperation of employers and the patriotic response of these young men, when the priority of need for their services as aircrew over that in industry is pointed out to them, will result in a new influx of recruits for flying training.
Generally speaking, the house can rest assured that every step will be taken and every effort will be made to see to it that Canada continues to supply an important quota to the air training plan and bearing in mind the fact, which has many times been stated in this house, that the field for aircrew recruiting is necessarily a restricted one, by reason of the requirements of age, fitness, mental alertness and motivation, Canada will continue to keep up the flow of pilots, navigators, air gunners, wireless operator air gunners, bombers, to our own R.C.A.F. squadrons and to the R.A.F. squadrons so that they will continue to strike the devastating blows which are shaking the axis powers to their very foundations.
Needless, to say, there is no battle between the army authorities and those of the R.C.A.F. We endeavour to work out our problems in a cooperative way, and the personnel and officers of the army and the R.C.A.F. are constantly meeting most amicably to that end. We may not always agree, but we are not fighting, and we hope by means of cooperation to work out our mutual problems satisfactorily.

With reference to the minister's statement in regard to the obtaining of aircrew, I have on my desk a letter from a young man, a graduate of McMaster university, who is very anxious to transfer from the army to the aircrew. He informs me that he has been making an effort for some time but has not been able to get anywhere. Could the minister advise me of any method which I could recommend to this young man whereby his desire might be satisfied.

There have been a number of cases of transfer, but my hon. friend and the public will understand that when men have trained for a considerable period for one arm of the service it does not seem to be desirable to have them transferred because they desire the change. If my hon. friend wishes to bring the case to my attention I shall be glad to look into it. Was he called up?
No.

If he was called up he had an opportunity of joining the air force

rather than the army prior to the time he actually reported for medical examination. He could have joined the air force instead of joining the army. Transfers are made even overseas from the army to the air force where men are specially fitted for the purpose or where there are circumstances which in the opinion of the army commander justify the change. Every case has to be dealt with on its merits.

I wondered what facilities were afforded to supply men from one branch to the other. It is a question of priority.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext: It is difficult for the army to enlist, train and post men for general service and then have them transfer to some other arm of the service. It would be only in special cases that this would be done, having regard to the army's own obligations and its own commitments, not only to our partners but to our men overseas. We have to provide reinforcements, and it is these very men whom we expect to provide those reinforcements.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I have no desire to delay the passing of these estimates; rather am I desirous of facilitating them so far as the national interest permits, but I should like to support what was said yesterday on the orders of the day by the hon. member for Broadview in regard to members of the Northwest Field Force. If I understand correctly the minister's explanation, these men as to pension are placed in the same position as any other soldiers who served in the South African campaign, the last war or, the present war, and I can quite see the minister's position in the technical answer he gave with regard to pensions. I am wondering, however, if there is not something that goes perhaps a little further than what has been actually discussed. These men served as early as 1885, if my memory serves me correctly.
Hon. IAN A. MACKENZIE (Minister of Pensions and National Health): That is correct.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I am wondering whether the difficulty may not arise to a large extent in connection with these men being able to attribute their disabilities to service in that particular theatre of war. That is one question I should like to ask the minister, because it may be germane to the discussion in regard to pensions for these men. It is hard enough to produce evidence of attributability in connection with the war which concluded twenty-five years ago. When one adds the years which have intervened since 4885 I have no doubt these men must find great difficulty in presenting any evidence on which they might base a claim that their disabilities are attributable to war service. That is the first point.
Then the minister raised a point in connection with the war veterans' allowance. As this committee well knows, the basis of a claim for the war veterans' allowance, or the burnt-out pension, as it is commonly called, is that the man must have seen service in an actual theatre of war, and it has been decided that those who saw service in England only in the last war may not properly apply for this allowance. I am not so sure that before long the minister will not have to review that position, but I do not want to bring that subject into this discussion. I do not believe the minister is confronted with an insurmountable difficulty in establishing an actual theatre of war in connection with the Northwest Field Force. It is true that this campaign was not on the scale of subsequent wars; nevertheless it was an important campaign from many
5362	COMMONS
Supply-Pensions and National Health
points of view. I should not think the minister would find it very difficult to have the northwest area established as an actual theatre of war. In effect it was a theatre of war, because fighting took place there.
The minister has given the technical reasons for not extending the war veterans' allowance to those who served in England during the last war. I am not arguing in favour of that at the moment, because I am afraid I have not always been able to see the distinction, but at least during the last war there was not hand to hand combat with the enemy on land in England. Perhaps the minister and the department have based their ruling in this connection on the fact that England could not be regarded technically as an actual theatre of war. But I take it that veterans of the South African war are entitled to apply for the war veterans' allowance; I believe that was provided in an amendment which was made not long ago. If the South African veterans are permitted to make application for this allowance, it seems to me that the distinction between their case and that of the Northwest Field Force is not very great. Certainly having in mind the number of these older, what we might call senior, veterans who would be involved, I am inclined to think that during the recess the minister might give careful consideration to the matter and if possible permit the war veterans' allowance to be extended to these men, not only by reason of their entitlement but for what I fancy would be another cogent reason, that is, the difficulty that most of these men will encounter in making application for pension in the ordinary way, in presenting proof of attribut-ability to war service. No such proof is required in connection with the war veterans' allowance, and the restrictions on the granting of that allowance are of course much less severe from the point of view of the applicant.
I want to place these points before the minister with great earnestness. There are not many of these veterans left, I think only some three hundred, and in all fairness to them we should take the position that they are entitled to make application now under the burnt-out pension arrangements, in view of the facts I have stated.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I have not the slightest fault to find with the remarks of my hon. friend; I think he has stated the position clearly and with accuracy. There would be no objection whatever to meeting this claim except for the implications that would be created in regard to other cases. After all, we have 193,105 men who served in Canada only during the last war. This claim is very small in itself; really it is largely

sentimental, because most of these men are entitled to the old age pension and I would imagine most of them are drawing that pension now. The benefit they would gain through coming under the veterans' allowance act would be very small; it would consist chiefly in the allowance to the widow for one year after death.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: They would be entitled to $40 a month, would they not?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: There would be a difference in the case of some married men. I think the issue is largely sentimental, and in themselves the financial considerations are very small indeed. It would mean, however, that later on the house would have to be prepared to meet the claims of those who had served only in Canada or England during the last war. It would be a measure of social security, and perhaps it will have to come, but that is the implication in doing this for these few survivors of the northwest rebellion. Personally I am not opposed to it at all. But I do say that the principle of veterans' allowances was that a man's age was shortened because of what he suffered in actual warfare, trench warfare, in the great war. It was considered that he was burnt-out and prematurely aged, and as such the old age pension was extended to him at an earlier age. Well, if that is to be extended for all the veterans of the great war, it is another matter. This request could easily be met, but it would involve a larger issue.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Is not the difference the fact that there was fighting in the northwest rebellion and that there was no fighting in Canada for the 193,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I do not think there were any conditions which prevailed in the northwest rebellion such as those which prevailed in trench warfare of the great war. There they had conditions which merited special consideration, the same as the veterans of the South African war. But there were no conditions in the northwest rebellion which would induce the introduction of a bill such as that which was passed in 1930, known as the War Veterans' Allowance Act. These men were prematurely aged by the stress and strain and terrible conditions which existed in the war of 1914-18.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I raised a purely hypothetical point, without having personal knowledge of the facts to which I alluded, other than by way of inference. These men experienced many difficulties in establishing their claim for pension, in view of the tremendous time which has elapsed.

Supply-
-Pensions and National Health

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: No, not the slightest. I do not know of one claim pending to-day. I do not think there is any difficulty at all about that. The whole thing is the suggestion that, having fought for Canada within Canada, they should have the same rights under this act as all other Canadian veterans.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: The minister has referred to the fighting in the great war. but I would point out that in the north-west rebellion there was fighting in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: There were many Canadians who served during the great war who are not eligible, under the act as we have it to-day.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
While the men who served in the Riel rebellion are certainly entitled to some compensation from the country for the services they rendered, I think that at this time to relate their service to disability from participation in a war is an impossibility. Furthermore, the condition in which these people now find themselves is a reflection on the government of that day. It is rather late to raise the question of pension for men who served during that time. Besides, I am opposed to shelving questions connected with social security by trying to dump them under the War Veterans' Allowance Act. In the past twenty-five years we have shirked our responsibility in the field of social security generally, by trying to handle the whole problem in a disjointed fashion. Under the act as it now stands, service in a theatre of war is not the only qualifying clause. The men who served in Canada or in England, if in receipt of a 5 per cent pension, are also entitled to veterans' allowance. I should imagine that if one were to go over the list of those in receipt of war veterans' allowance he would find as many men on that list, as many men who served in Canada and in England, as there are men who served overseas in a theatre of war.
My experience has been that, by and large, the men who served in a theatre of war are regular pensioners. The other measure was brought in to cover men who suffered disease and disability which could not be attributed to service. I am absolutely opposed to classifying the War Veterans' Allowance Act as an old age pension act. I believe too much of that sort of thing is being done. In many instances war veterans, who come under the war veterans' allowance provisions, are being injured because the provinces and the federal government are using the War Veterans' Allowance Act as an old age pension measure.
I have run into cases of the kind on several occasions, and I have no doubt the minister has too. The provincial government pays an old age pension to a wife, for example, of $15 or $20 a month. When the veterans' allowance is granted to the husband, instead of getting the $40 a month to which he is entitled under the act, the amount of the old age pension being paid in the province is deducted. This militates against the soldier, because it is being used as an old age pension.
I think the minister was correct when he said it is generally recognized by medical authorities that a man's life is shortened, by at least ten years, as a result of war service, and certain provision was made under the act to enable the veterans to receive something at the age of sixty. But I do not think it was ever the intention to deduct from the veterans the amount paid by the provinces to other members of a family by way of old age pension. The men who took part in the Riel rebellion were the victims of a faulty system; their position is a glaring example of the lack of interest on the part of past governments, and this is something which will have to be taken care of.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Would my hon. hon. friend permit an interruption? He referred to the number of recipients under the War Veterans' Allowance Act. There were 1,841 who served in Canada and England only, out of a total of 24,192.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: The point I wished to make, for the benefit of the leader of the opposition, was that overseas service in a theatre of actual war was not the only qualifying clause.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Correct.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: In my opinion the men who served in the Riel rebellion, and any others in that category, will have to be covered by social security. I believe that is the answer to the question. This procedure of dumping everything into the Department of Pensions and National Health, as we have been doing for the past twenty-five years because there has been nowhere else to go, is bad practice. If the leader of the opposition is interested- and I know he is-he would do well to hold up both hands in support of a social security programme.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
There is one matter which I believe should be considered, and might best be considered under this item. May I first however refer briefly to what has been said by the minister and the hon. member for Cape Breton South with regard to the inadvisability of dumping into the War
5364	COMMONS
Supply-Pensions and National Health
Veterans' Allowance Act problems having to do with social security. I should be inclined to agree with both of them, provided there were any immediate possibility of having social security in this country. But what is now happening, and has been happening for years, is that these men who fought, bled and now suffer are being allowed to go without the necessities of life, while Canada waits upon the introduction of a measure of social security. By the time we have adequate social security most of these men will be in their graves, and we shall have committed what in my judgment is a national crime. I have felt ever since these men went to war and returned from it that it was Canada's duty to take care of them. Never mind social security; if we cannot get it, at least let us take care of these men and their dependents.
Another matter I should like to discuss briefly is one which I hestitate to discuss at this late stage in the session, but one concerning which I believe something must be said. On July 12, when the Prime Minister was giving one of his glowing speeches, I rose and reminded him that Canada had not played fair with her returned men. The Prime Minister made remarks which indicated that I was making innuendoes and insinuations which I ought not to make without having sufficient evidence to support my statement. Before we finished the little passage between myself and the Prime Minister I promised that I would bring forth evidence before this session was over in full support of my statement. My words, as reported on page 4622 of Hansard were:
If I have said anything up to the present time which either by implication or by meaning could be construed as offensive or as inappropriate on this occasion, I withdraw it; but I give assurance to the house that at a later time I shall reassert it, because so far as I am concerned, Mr. Speaker, as one member of parliament I do not propose to neglect my bounden duty to the people who sent me here and to the soldiers who are fighting our war.
First of all, I shall read a quotation from a letter for which I vouch, which I have right here, written by a veteran of both wars. This letter is dated July 13, so that evidently this man lost no time sending it in. I have others, but I think this is probably better by far than anything else I have. I read:
In the first place I should tell you who I am and what authority I have for making these statements. I am a doctor of twenty-two years' experience. I served as a doctor in the last war and did not get overseas because of the influenza epidemic. I also served in this war but did not get overseas.
While serving at the Atlantic coast in various units I saw examined and boarded for discharge many fine young men who entered the active 
army-they were not draftees. These men were often subjected to rainy, foggy weather, often getting their clothes wet while guarding a coast so that our premier as well as all could rest in peace.
Many of these boys were on active service at the coast two years or more. Suddenly they get a terrible cold, fever and sore throat, tonsilitis or septic sore throat, followed by rheumatic fever or rheumatic arthritis.
May I interject here that even though these boys who are afflicted in this manner may not have seen the heat of battle, they have made a sacrifice for the country which puts the country under an obligation to see that they are provided for. I go on with the letter.
The policy of the army and government has been to date to discharge these men, one month's post discharge pay and to hell with them any more.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: That is entirely wrong.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: This is a statement by a man who has been right through it.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: He does not know anything about it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I do not see how a man could know anything more about it than the man who had boarded these men.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I am sorry to disagree with my hon. friend.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I am glad to hear the minister say that. I shall go on with the letter.
Our government has taken the stand that there is no pension for service in Canada if disabled by disease.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: That is not correct either.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
The letter continues:
I ask you or any person in the democratic world if that is what we are fighting for? Every good soldier does what he is ordered to do. If sent overseas, he goes. If detailed for coast protection-then he does it. Why should any soldier on active service be penalized because his health broke down by service in Canada? I will except all venereal diseases.
I claim that all men are examined by men who are appointed by the military authorities who in turn are acting for the government. I claim that if once accepted and health breaks under the strain of the changed life that the government is responsible. I myself had an attack of coronary thrombosis and have not been able to do any work since. I have talked to 

.
I am going to leave out some names, but I can supply them privately to the minister.
I think it is just as well that these names should not appear on Hansard because there will be plenty of malodorous results from some of these things. "I continue:

Supply-Pensions and National Health
This man has a nose like Major Hoople and shows that he is more interested in something else. He has never had a private practice of his own and has served for too many years. He even refused me a rehabilitation grant. I tried to take a post-graduate course after my discharge so I attended 

 university.
I am leaving out the name of the university. I continue:
Studying is mental work but not physical. I secured my D.P.H. degree (Doctor of Public Health) and I also have my L.G.M.C. All these are no good to me because I thought that I could do work if I removed the night calls.
Apparently this man found himself unequal to the task of carrying on even after he had done all he possibly could to prepare himself. The latter continues:
However, the refusal of rehabilitation was made direct by 

.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Is he referring to the rehabilitation grant paid by the army, or to the rehabilitation benefits paid by this department?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: All I know is what appears in the letter, and it is not sufficiently definite to enable me to answer the minister's question. I shall place this letter in the minister's hands so that he can examine it. A member of parliament, generally speaking, receiving a thing like this is in duty bound to consider it. I am simply passing it on. If I receive a letter of this sort from a man who looks dependable I think I ought to bring it up.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Has the hon. member brought this letter to my attention before now?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
No, I did not bring this to the minister's attention, largely because of the lateness of the session. I have brought cases to the minister's attention and although he has shown a lot of sympathy I have felt that he was bound by some hidden hand and I pretty well lost heart about taking things up with him.
I should like to read a passage from another letter for which I am prepared to vouch. This is by a veteran of the two wars. He says:
To-day, as always, you can look around you and see the poverty and rags of these veterans from the trenches. The deaf and disabled refused a pension and their pensions and their job handed out to a non-combatant for political reasons.
I cannot vouch for the statement regarding political reasons. I like to keep free of all offensive things like political struggles. I abhor them, I despise them, but they are there and I can do nothing about them. I am not going to talk about them, but this is this man's statement:
These men never out of Canada are not war veterans.
I do not know that I agree with the writer there.
They were never in the war. Recently there was a job open in Woodstock. The civil service made a big time. They need not have bothered. We veterans know. The man appointed got as far as England, says Ottawa. To England where we went on leave; to England where we went for fun, pastime and amusement; to England where we went when we were sick and wounded. We went. We, the slackers from the trenches. God save England. These men never out of Canada and those that got as far as England did nothing but eat our rations and take our jobs and our pensions. They met us when we were coming back.
Those are bitter words, but let it be borne in mind that they come from the lips of a veteran of the two wars.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: He is not complaining of this department; he is complaining of the civil service commission.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Possibly, but there are other things that apply to this department. I continue:
The Pension Act states: "That a pension should not be denied the veteran because no disabling condition existed at time of discharge". Just try and get it. His papers come back from Ottawa marked "Application refused" and no reason given except from some previous examination years before. If they did not intend to examine the veteran, why call him before the board, and having given him no examination on what do they base their claim of "Application refused'"? You don't know and neither does the veteran, and this way of handling the veteran has not helped in any way, but only filled him with bitterness, and you can expect nothing else from disabled veterans who watch their families grow up in poverty unable to pay their way for the necessities of life, unable to secure employment on account of war handicaps and knowing of the graft in pensions and jobs handed out for political reward while we continue in our poverty, denied justice or assistance from the country we fought for. Is that what you have in store for those now fighting?
This is a lengthy document and I do not propose to read any more from it. I am sorry to say that my own experience of the treatment accorded to many veterans to whose cases I have endeavoured to have some consideration given has led me to sympathize with the remarks in this document. I will not say that the statements therein are entirely accurate but I will say that there is a cheeseparing, niggardly, inhuman way of dealing with veterans of this war which leaves much to be desired. I lay no blame on the men who are trying to administer the act; I am not in a position to blame them. I do not know that I would blame the minister. I think what we have to do is to blame the whole general
5366	COMMONS
Supply-Pensions and National Health
attitude which seems to fill the mind of the government and seems to fill too many minds in this country-an attitude which endeavours to treat these men just as cheaply and as niggardly as we possibly can and still get by under the act.
I have had experience in my own constituency with men whose treatment simply revolted every fibre of my being. Let me mention one of them. Just this last year he was receiving a war veteran's allowance. I do not think I had better give any details about what this man is doing, because I find that when knowledge comes to be had regarding some of these men they do not get on so well after that. This man is in receipt of a war veteran's allowance. The way in which the inspectors go around and poke their noses into his affairs and watch and scrutinize every little movement he makes for fear he is going to make five or ten cents more than what the act says he can is simply astounding. This man said he had a chance this year-I am not going to tell what the work was

to go and do some very necessary war work in connection with agriculture. He could work in the harvest field-I will go mo further. This man could have had about fifteen days' work, but if I remember correctly he had to stop work at five and a half days of work. He was quite able to do the work out in the fields, and the farmer needed him, but he had to stop work at five and a half days, or some of his war veteran's allowance would! be sneaked away from him on the plea that he had1 accepted more than the amount of money which the law laid down as being the limit. I am not going to say that the men who were administering the law were not strictly within their rights, but I say that a government that takes such an attitude and forces its officers to take it certainly has a whole lot to learn.
I think the minister is doing everything in his power to make the act better. I am not complaining against him at all; I want him to understand that. But he knows certainly how many, many things in this country ought to be made right in order to give the men who fought our war last time and the men who are fighting our war this time anything like a fair chance.
I believe, Mr. Chairman, that I have said enough to support what I said to the Prime Minister, and I will say no more, except that I hope this house will see that a great .deal more generous treatment is meted out to every man who served in the last war and to every man who serves in this war.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I am not going to make a speech at this stage. I merely want to inform the hon. member for Lethbridge that the instructions issued throughout the Department of Pensions and National Health are that every possible consideration must be given to every individual case. These are the instructions given by the minister, and these are the instructions carried out by all members and staff of the pension board and all the veterans' allowance boards. Every single member of these boards is a veteran of the great war. In the four years that I have been in the department I have found nothing but the utmost desire to administer all the statutes and the regulations for the benefit of the veteran and his dependents.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Within certain financial limitations.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: There are no financial limitations placed on the Department of Pensions and National Health in administering the act.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: You have only so much money to spend.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
We get estimates of what is required from our own experts and they have never Been turned down. Never has an estimate that has been brought in for pensions been turned down-never. In regard to health, yes, but in regard to pensions, never. Certain principles have been established by parliament, and within the ambit of the statute and the regulations we have never by virtue of financial considerations been denied by any government- this applies to former governments as well as this one-anything we required. I have found in this house all the time I have been here a unanimous desire upon the part of all members to do everything possible for these men. There are bound to be cases of hardship, but when they are brought to my attention every single thing that it is possible to do is done and will be done to provide a remedy.
The amazing thing is this. We have the best pension act and the best war veterans' allowance act, passed by all parties in the house, not only in the British empire but among the united nations as well, and in our preparations for rehabilitation we are ahead of the empire and all the united nations. When the empire parliamentary delegation were here they were immediate in their acceptance of that fact when they saw what we are trying to do. I am the first one to want to remedy any case of hardship. It is not a

Supply-Pensions and National Health
matter of government but of parliament and the humanitarian heart of this house. If there are any cases of hardship, and I include the cases wihich my hon. friend has mentioned which 'had not been brought to my attention before, they will be remedied if I have the power so to do. Anything that we can do for the men who fought the last war and for the men who are fighting this war and their dependents will be done.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I am not going to make a speech, but I cannot let the statements that have been made by the hon. member for Lethbridge go without a protest. As a veteran of the last war I want to say that his statements are a reflection on the men who fought in the last war and on all those who are administering pension legislation. It is unfair to those gentlemen to say that the administration of this act is niggardly or inhuman or something for which we should bow our heads in shame. Instead of reading extracts from letters which are not tabled, the names of whose writers are not given, if he would take those letters over to the commission, as other hon. members do, and get the other side, he would find that every man employed in the department is at all times most sympathetic and most willing to go very carefully into every case. I regret that circulation throughout the country should be given to remarks which are a reflection upon the administration of this act by a staff who, within the limits of this act which was passed by parliament after it was gone into thoroughly by a committee composed entirely of veterans of the last war, are giving the most sympathetic and generous administration which under the act can possibly be given.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: There is one point I would like to draw to the minister's attention at this time. Under the Pensions Act as it is to-day, soldiers serving in Canada who become disabled are pensionable only if their dependents are in necessitous circumstances. I should like the minister to define exactly what is meant by "necessitous circumstances." Does it mean, for instance, that the soldier is an indigent? The minister will remember that during the sessions of the committee last year we discussed the question of free hospitalization, and it was stated that any soldier who was an indigent could receive free hospitalization. I asked, I think it was, Doctor Miller, to define "indigent", and he said, any soldier with an income of less than $1,000 a year. What I want to know from the minister is, will any soldier with an income of less than 81,000 a year be granted a pension provided he becomes disabled while serving in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I am not personally aware of the criterion that is being used by the board of pension commissioners. I am aware of the instructions which were given to them after section 11, subsection 3, was passed, and that was to be as liberal and generous as they possibly could in the interpretation of that section. I would have to consult the chairman of the pensions commission, who unfortunately is ill at the moment, with regard to the exact criterion they use in defining necessitous circumstances.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: The minister would admit that if a soldier is indigent he would be in necessitous circumstances, and if that has been defined as represented by an income of less than $1,000, that should be the criterion by which we should judge necessitous circumstances. Have any applications for pensions been refused on the ground that a soldier was not in necessitous circumstances?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: I am informed that there have been some. The percentage I have not under my hand; I shall be glad to get it for my hon. friend.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
A good deal of the discussion we have had to-day and on other occasions as to whether or not veterans are getting proper treatment really relates to the terms of the act itself. We have been told this morning that the best possible administration is being given within the terms of the act. Has not the minister as the result of his experience realized the necessity, if not the desirability, of making changes in the act so as to make it possible to extend better treatment to veterans of the last war? I have in mind the kind of case of which we receive a great many, and refer them to the department and to the minister. I have a notion that the minister is sympathetic to our point of view. Often, where the pensionable disability resulting from the last war was minor, the amount the man is receiving is not sufficient to live on, and in recent years other disabilities have developed; and to a layman, to the veteran himself, to his friends, to anyone looking at it from a nonmedical and non-technical point of view, it seems clear that the man's condition has deteriorated and that really it relates to his services in the last war. When we take it up with the department we get reconsideration, the case is looked into, but in due course case after case is turned down on medical grounds. We go to the minister and we are told that the best has been done within the act as passed by this parliament. Like other hon. members, I have many cases

I wish to say a word with regard to section 32(a) as applied to widows who do not come under the arrangements now made under the additional appropriation to provide for those whose husbands might have qualified under the War Veteran's Allowance Act. There are a large number of women in Canada who are in poor circumstances and who are not provided for yet. With regard to section 32(a) and the limitation it places upon certain classifications of widows, women who marry after the time limit was set, to all intents and purposes these women are single so far as the pension regulations are concerned. There was quite a long discussion on section 32(a) before the pensions committee when it sat, revising and bringing up to date the Pension Act, and strong recommendations were made to the minister for the removal of section 32(a), or at least to bring it into conformity with the act as it applies now to the widows of veterans of this war. The recommendation was made that where they were in necessitous circumstances, regardless of that time limitation, they should be given the privilege extended to widows of this war.
One important matter I would bring to the minister's attention is this. Many veterans of the last war who came back suffering mentally
were not provided with any kind of institution except the ordinary mental institutions of the country. I had the privilege of visiting one and I felt that it was certainly a lack of foresight on the part of the Canadian government to take men who were not insane in the real sense of the word, but merely suffering from shock, and put them in with mental patients of all descriptions. It is a horrible condition for a man to be placed in after receiving the shock he did while fighting for his country.
Listening to the Minister of National Defence for Air, I thought he made a very kindly statement. He pointed out that this was a shock war and therefore the problem of mental cases coming back will be magnified one hundred per cent. That applies particularly to the boys in the air. He pointed out that great difficulty was being experienced. Many of these boys who are coming back from service over there are in such a condition that it is hard to place them, and as time goes on, if that disability is not taken care of properly, I am afraid that we shall have to build mental institutions in this country. I suggest that the matter be taken into consideration and that proper neurological hospitals be established, with trained staffs to take care of cases of this kind.
I have a suggestion to offer. The statement of the Minister of National Defence for Air has proven conclusively, to my mind at any rate, that from the point of view of medical science, it is not certain what can be done with such cases. I suggest to the minister that as regards the air force boys now returning, every possible means that might be provided to bring relief to these boys should be studied. Two or three cases should be taken as test cases and chiropractic used in order to bring relief. I remember some years ago when the Chiropractic Association of Ontario made an offer to the provincial government. They were prepared to go to the mental institutions of the province in order to become legally qualified to practise in Ontario, and they said that they would make a test, guaranteeing to turn out of the mental institutions a certain percentage of cases as cured. That was to be the test. I do not know anything about it, but the Minister of National Defence for Air proved conclusively to me' that so far as those cases that are now coming back are concerned, there is nothing to-day that will bring them relief. The whole matter is in the experimental stage. We should not lose any bets in trying all the facilities we have in order to bring some relief to these boys. I do not know anything
